content:
Northstar Fintech x Redwood — Predictive Autoscaling technical deep dive
Recorded: 2025-06-03 16:02 UTC
Duration: 53 minutes

Attendees
- Redwood Inference: Liam O'Rourke, Vanessa Ortiz, Keiko Yamamoto, Sana Farid
- Northstar Fintech: Ava Chen (Platform Eng), Mark Feldman (SRE), Priya Shah (FinOps), Daniel Kim (ML Platform)

Auto-generated summary (Fireflies)
Northstar described predictable daily traffic ramps (market open / batch jobs) that currently cause queue build-up before reactive autoscaling catches up. They want a configurable lead time for pre-scaling, plus hard spend guardrails via max capacity bounds. Redwood walked through an approach where a predictive signal can “bias” desired replicas, but reactive signals (queue depth / saturation) still override incorrect predictions while respecting customer min/max bounds. The teams discussed acceptable overshoot thresholds, staleness/fallback behavior, and how audit logs + dashboards would show requested vs bounded capacity.

Topics
- Northstar ramp patterns + lead time needs
- Defining acceptable overshoot and safe baseline min
- How predictive signals interact with reactive autoscaling
- Bounds (min/max) semantics and precedence
- Failure modes: stale predictions, region capacity shortages, oscillation
- Observability and auditability for enterprise

Questions captured
- Can predictive scaling ever exceed max? (No; max is a hard clamp.)
- If prediction is missing/null, do we scale down? (No; revert to reactive; never unsafe downscale.)
- Can we set different policies per deployment/region? (Yes per deployment; region behavior depends on Dedicated topology.)
- What’s the recommended minimum baseline for “no cold start” during ramp? (Workload-dependent; Redwood proposed starting from current steady-state + safety margin.)

Transcript

[00:00] Liam O'Rourke: Alright, I think we’re good to go. This is Liam from Redwood. Thanks everyone for making time. The goal today is basically to go one level deeper on predictive autoscaling—what you need for market open ramps, what lead time, what you consider acceptable overshoot, and then we’ll propose how we’d do it with guardrails.

[00:18] Ava Chen: Sounds good.

[00:19] Mark Feldman: Yep.

[00:21] Liam O'Rourke: Vanessa and Keiko are here from our fleet autoscaling side, and Sana from… forecasting evaluation. If it’s okay, Ava, maybe you start with your ramp pattern—like what does a “bad day” look like.

[00:34] Ava Chen: Sure. So, we have two predictable ramps. One is market open. We’re US equities heavy so 9:30 Eastern. We see traffic start rising around 9:15, and by like 9:28 it’s basically already spiking.

[00:51] Daniel Kim: Yeah and sometimes there’s like pre-market news and it’s earlier.

[00:55] Ava Chen: Right. But consistent is 9:15 to 9:35. Our current scaling is reactive on CPU and queue length, and it’s just… it catches up at like 9:40.

[01:06] Mark Feldman: And that means p95 latency goes from 900ms to like 3–4 seconds during that window. Some requests time out.

[01:14] Liam O'Rourke: Got it. And this is on the inference tier, your LLM inference.

[01:18] Ava Chen: Yeah. The service that calls the model for summarization and a classification step.

[01:23] Priya Shah: And the cost pain is the flipside. If we set static capacity to cover that, we pay all day. So we want it to come up before the ramp, then come down after.

[01:35] Vanessa Ortiz: That’s exactly the shape predictive helps with: pre-warm capacity ahead of a known ramp. Quick check—are you currently on our Hosted API or looking at Dedicated.

[01:43] Ava Chen: We’re in POC for Dedicated. We have compliance requirements and also we want predictable throughput. Hosted is okay for dev.

[01:52] Liam O'Rourke: Yep, makes sense.

[01:54] Vanessa Ortiz: Okay. So in Dedicated, the autoscaler’s “unit” is replicas—each replica maps to a GPU slice or full GPU depending on the model config. The knobs you’re asking for are: minimum baseline, a maximum cap, and then predictive mode which can push desired replicas up ahead of time.

[02:13] Mark Feldman: But it can’t blow past the cap. That’s kind of the non-negotiable thing.

[02:17] Vanessa Ortiz: Totally. We treat max as a hard clamp. Desired comes in, we clamp it.

[02:23] Priya Shah: Can we define max in dollars? Or only in GPUs.

[02:27] Keiko Yamamoto: Initially it’s capacity units—replica count / GPU quota. Console can show estimated spend impact, but enforcement is capacity-based.

[02:36] Priya Shah: Okay, but we can translate to spend with a fixed price per GPU hour. That’s fine.

[02:42] Liam O'Rourke: We can help with the mapping.

[02:45] Sana Farid: Maybe to anchor it: the “overshoot” question becomes “how much above the ramp do you want us to pre-scale”, right? If you tell us you can tolerate +10% extra for 20 minutes, that’s a bounded cost.

[02:56] Ava Chen: Right. I think +10% for a short time is fine. It’s the “runaway scale” we’ve been burned by.

[03:03] Mark Feldman: Yeah, like a feedback loop where latency increases, queue grows, it scales, and then it keeps scaling because queue is still high. Then the spike ends and you’re stuck.

[03:12] Vanessa Ortiz: Yeah, the classic. Two things we do: cooldowns and dampening. And with predictive we also do “do no harm” style: if predictions are missing or obviously stale we fall back to reactive. And reactive has its own safety invariants.

[03:26] Daniel Kim: When you say stale, what’s the threshold.

[03:29] Keiko Yamamoto: We typically define a “forecast timestamp” and a “valid_until”. Like, if the forecast is older than, say, 15 minutes for a 15-min lead-time policy, we consider it stale.

[03:39] Mark Feldman: And if stale, you just… ignore it.

[03:41] Keiko Yamamoto: Ignore it and rely on reactive signals.

[03:44] Ava Chen: So we don’t scale down based on missing forecast.

[03:48] Keiko Yamamoto: Correct. We never do an unsafe downscale because a predictor returned null. (I’m emphasizing because we’ve seen that bug class.)

[03:56] Liam O'Rourke: Keiko’s referencing a general class, not you specifically.

[04:00] Ava Chen: No I appreciate it.

[04:02] Sana Farid: Can you share what lead time is actually helpful? Like if we pre-scale 5 minutes early, is that enough or do you need 20.

[04:10] Ava Chen: For GPUs, it depends. We’ve seen “cold start” for loading weights—like 6 to 10 minutes.

[04:18] Daniel Kim: If it has to pull from registry or load into VRAM, yeah.

[04:22] Vanessa Ortiz: In Dedicated we try to keep the image and weights local, but the model initialization still takes time. For your model size, what are you running.

[04:31] Daniel Kim: We’re testing Llama 3 70B quantized, and then a smaller 8B. The 70B is the one that hurts.

[04:38] Vanessa Ortiz: Yeah. For that, we generally recommend 10–15 minutes lead time to avoid queue buildup.

[04:46] Mark Feldman: So we’d want to pre-scale starting 9:15 for 9:30.

[04:49] Vanessa Ortiz: Exactly.

[04:51] Priya Shah: Then the question is: how do we tell you “market open daily” so it’s deterministic, vs purely learned from history.

[04:59] Liam O'Rourke: Great question. We’ve been discussing two modes. One is scheduled events—like you define a schedule: weekdays 9:15 to 9:45 Eastern, add +N replicas. That’s the simplest and most deterministic.

[05:13] Ava Chen: That’s kinda what I want.

[05:14] Liam O'Rourke: The second is forecasting based on historical demand. That’s “predictive” in the ML sense. The project we’re working on is more the second, but we can also treat schedules as an input signal.

[05:28] Sana Farid: Right, schedule is like a perfect feature. But we still need guardrails because sometimes holidays, or half days, or you have an outage.

[05:36] Mark Feldman: Yeah or we don’t want it to scale up on Christmas.

[05:39] Keiko Yamamoto: So the autoscaler evaluates: reactive desired, predictive desired, then it chooses a combined desired. Then clamps to [min,max].

[05:50] Ava Chen: How does it choose combined desired. Like max of the two.

[05:55] Vanessa Ortiz: Usually it’s “take the higher” for scale-up, because if either says we need more, we’d rather be safe. But we also keep a rule: if reactive says you’re already saturated—queue depth, GPU utilization, etc.—we can ignore a lower predictive suggestion. Predictive can’t force you down during load.

[06:13] Mark Feldman: And scale-down.

[06:15] Vanessa Ortiz: Scale-down is more conservative. We enforce cooldowns and step-down limits.

[06:21] Sana Farid: This gets to oscillation. If the prediction bounces, we don’t want replica counts bouncing every minute.

[06:27] Daniel Kim: Yeah, we’ve seen “sawtooth” patterns.

[06:30] Keiko Yamamoto: Exactly. We can configure a minimum interval between scale actions and a minimum step size. So like “no more than one scale-down every 10 minutes”, and “don’t scale down by more than 10% in one action.”

[06:44] Ava Chen: Is that per deployment.

[06:46] Keiko Yamamoto: Yes, per deployment policy.

[06:49] Liam O'Rourke: Let’s double-click on acceptable overshoot. Priya, you said +10% okay. Is that in replica count or spend.

[06:56] Priya Shah: Spend. But we can translate. Suppose our steady state is 20 GPUs. During market open we might need 40. If you pre-scale to 45 for 20 minutes, that’s maybe okay. Pre-scale to 70 is not.

[07:12] Sana Farid: So for evaluation we’d call that “overshoot ratio”: (provisioned - required) / required. You’re saying keep it under ~10–15% and also duration limited.

[07:22] Priya Shah: Exactly.

[07:24] Mark Feldman: Another thing: we need to avoid queueing. If the model gets backed up, it takes like 30 minutes to recover even after scaling.

[07:32] Vanessa Ortiz: That’s pretty common because the backlog itself creates lag. One of our primary success metrics in predictive is “time to prevent queue”: you pre-scale so queue depth stays near zero.

[07:42] Ava Chen: What signals do you use for reactive. GPU utilization seems weird sometimes because it’s batched.

[07:49] Vanessa Ortiz: Yep, utilization is noisy with continuous batching. We prefer queue depth and request latency. But we normalize for model and batch settings.

[07:58] Mark Feldman: We can provide queue metrics from our gateway.

[08:01] Keiko Yamamoto: That’s helpful. We also have internal queue depth in the serving runtime. Sometimes people call it “pending tokens.”

[08:08] Daniel Kim: KV cache—does that affect scaling? Because if you scale down you lose cache and then you get slower again.

[08:15] Vanessa Ortiz: Yes, KV cache can make it sticky. It’s one reason scale-down is conservative. In some cases we’ll keep a baseline min above 1 so you don’t churn cache. (Sorry, transcription might say “KV cash”.)

[08:28] Liam O'Rourke: Just to keep us oriented: the product feature we’re building is min/max bounds plus predictive mode. That’s what would let you set baseline 20, max 45, predictive lead time 15 minutes, and safety. That’s what we’re proposing for your pilot.

[08:46] Ava Chen: Good.

[08:47] Mark Feldman: What about if the region doesn’t have GPUs. Like we set min 20 and you can’t actually give us 20.

[08:54] Vanessa Ortiz: Great question. In Dedicated, your capacity is reserved, so for the reserved pool we should be able to meet min. But if you set a min above your contracted pool, or during a partial outage, then we can’t. In that case we surface a “min unmet” degraded state and alert.

[09:10] Mark Feldman: That alert goes to us.

[09:12] Keiko Yamamoto: It can page Redwood SRE first, and optionally notify you in Console / webhook. We’re still finalizing, but the key is it’s explicit and audit logged.

[09:22] Ava Chen: Audit logged is important for us, because we have change management.

[09:25] Liam O'Rourke: Yep. We can record who changed min/max, when, and then scaling decisions: requested desired, bounded desired, and the reason code.

[09:36] Priya Shah: Reason code like “hit max cap”.

[09:38] Keiko Yamamoto: Exactly. “bounded_by_max”, “bounded_by_min”, “forecast_stale_fallback”, “reactive_override_queue”, things like that.

[09:48] Sana Farid: On the forecasting side, we also track prediction error—so later we can see if it’s doing the right thing.

[09:55] Daniel Kim: What do you need from us to build the forecast.

[09:59] Sana Farid: Ideally per-minute request rate and maybe tokens per request distribution, at least percentiles, because GPU load depends on tokens not just requests.

[10:09] Ava Chen: We can share aggregated.

[10:11] Sana Farid: That’s fine. Even a “tokens per minute” time series is good.

[10:16] Liam O'Rourke: Mark, what’s your desired SLO. Like p95 target.

[10:21] Mark Feldman: For that summarization call, p95 under 1.2 seconds. We can tolerate p99 at 2.5 for a short time.

[10:30] Vanessa Ortiz: And today during ramp you said p95 3–4 seconds.

[10:33] Mark Feldman: Correct.

[10:35] Vanessa Ortiz: Okay. That’s an easy “win” if predictive is stable.

[10:38] Ava Chen: But we also don’t want to just scale up huge. Like we need a deterministic cap.

[10:44] Liam O'Rourke: Understood. Let’s do a concrete example. Suppose at 9:30 you need 40 replicas. We set max 45. Predictive says scale to 42 at 9:15. Reactive says scale to 38 at 9:20 because it sees early load. Then combined desired becomes 42 (max of the two). Then clamp to max 45. So you’re at 42, good.

[11:06] Mark Feldman: And if prediction says 55.

[11:08] Keiko Yamamoto: Then bounded desired is 45, reason “bounded_by_max.” And we can show you that.

[11:14] Priya Shah: Good.

[11:15] Ava Chen: If you hit max and queue builds, what happens.

[11:19] Vanessa Ortiz: Then you’re in a “saturated at max” state. We alert. Routing can also degrade gracefully—like if you have a fallback model or lower tier. But we can’t exceed your max.

[11:31] Daniel Kim: That’s fine. We’d rather degrade than exceed spend.

[11:35] Liam O'Rourke: That’s consistent with what we’ve heard from other fintechs.

[11:40] Sana Farid: We should also talk about the second ramp you mentioned.

[11:43] Ava Chen: The batch job. It’s 5pm Eastern, like 4:50 to 5:20. It’s not as spiky but it’s consistent. That’s more internal usage.

[11:54] Mark Feldman: And occasionally on earnings days there’s a third spike around 4:05.

[11:59] Sana Farid: That’s where a schedule feed could help—earnings calendar.

[12:03] Daniel Kim: We do have an internal “events” service.

[12:06] Liam O'Rourke: If you can give us a webhook or even a manual schedule for pilot, we can incorporate as an input.

[12:13] Ava Chen: For pilot, simplest is just the daily schedule.

[12:16] Vanessa Ortiz: Perfect.

[12:18] Mark Feldman: One concern: time zones. We’ve been bit by UTC offsets.

[12:22] Keiko Yamamoto: Yeah, we require timezone explicitly in config. And we store schedules normalized. Also, all our logs show UTC plus the configured TZ.

[12:31] Ava Chen: Good.

[12:32] Priya Shah: Can we update these settings via Terraform.

[12:35] Liam O'Rourke: Not on day one, but it’s on the roadmap. For now, Console and API. For enterprise we can work with you.

[12:43] Priya Shah: Okay.

[12:45] Vanessa Ortiz: Another safety topic: config churn. If someone keeps editing min/max, you can get unstable behavior.

[12:51] Mark Feldman: Yeah, or an automation script goes wild.

[12:54] Keiko Yamamoto: We can rate limit policy changes and also audit log them. So you’d see it.

[13:01] Liam O'Rourke: Let’s talk about “minimum baseline.” Ava, if you had to choose a min, what would you set.

[13:06] Ava Chen: Probably our steady state plus a little. Maybe 20.

[13:11] Daniel Kim: It depends on which model is pinned. If it’s the 70B it needs more.

[13:16] Vanessa Ortiz: We can set min per deployment, and deployments can map to different models. So you might set min 10 for 8B service, min 20 for 70B.

[13:27] Mark Feldman: Do you do separate deployments per model.

[13:29] Liam O'Rourke: Usually yes in Dedicated, because capacity planning is different.

[13:33] Sana Farid: For the predictive part, the forecast is per deployment too.

[13:38] Ava Chen: Okay.

[13:40] Mark Feldman: How do you validate the predictor isn’t totally wrong.

[13:44] Sana Farid: During pilot we’d run it in “shadow” first—compute predicted desired, but not apply it. Then compare. Once it’s within error thresholds, we enable it.

[13:56] Mark Feldman: Nice. That’s what we do with some of our internal stuff.

[13:59] Vanessa Ortiz: And even when enabled, reactive can override if reality diverges.

[14:05] Daniel Kim: Can you define override precisely.

[14:08] Keiko Yamamoto: Sure. Example: prediction says you only need 30 but queue depth is rising, reactive says 40. Then we take 40. Prediction never forces you lower when you’re saturated. That’s our invariant.

[14:23] Mark Feldman: Good.

[14:24] Ava Chen: But can prediction force you higher even if reactive says lower.

[14:28] Vanessa Ortiz: Yes, that’s the point—pre-scale. We’ll take the higher for scale up, within max.

[14:35] Priya Shah: As long as max is hard.

[14:36] Vanessa Ortiz: Max is hard.

[14:38] Liam O'Rourke: I want to capture the lead time. You said 10 minutes for weight load, but safer 15.

[14:43] Ava Chen: Yeah, 15.

[14:45] Sana Farid: Great. We can set “lead_time_minutes=15” and evaluate forecast at least every minute but with smoothing.

[14:52] Daniel Kim: Every minute seems like it could flap.

[14:55] Sana Farid: The forecast output can update every minute, but the autoscaler doesn’t need to act every minute. It can hold unless change exceeds threshold.

[15:04] Keiko Yamamoto: Exactly. We separate “decision loop” and “actuation.” Actuation is rate-limited.

[15:12] Mark Feldman: Okay.

[15:13] Liam O'Rourke: Are there constraints on maximum scale-up per step. Like do you prefer a single jump vs gradual.

[15:21] Mark Feldman: For us, faster is better, but we’ve seen big jumps cause scheduling issues.

[15:27] Vanessa Ortiz: On GPU fleets, big jumps can cause thundering herd on scheduling and model init. So we often do staged scale-up: step of, say, 20% every couple minutes until target.

[15:40] Ava Chen: That’s fine as long as it’s early enough.

[15:43] Vanessa Ortiz: Right. That’s why lead time.

[15:46] Priya Shah: Can we set different max for weekdays vs weekends.

[15:50] Keiko Yamamoto: Not initially. But you can have schedules that change desired, and max stays the hard cap. Some customers set max to worst-case and use schedule for normal.

[16:02] Priya Shah: Hmm. We’d want max lower on weekends because spend is scrutinized.

[16:06] Liam O'Rourke: Understood. For pilot, we can keep it simple with one max, and then see if you need “time-based max” later.

[16:13] Ava Chen: Okay.

[16:15] Mark Feldman: Security: does the predictor see our data.

[16:18] Liam O'Rourke: Just metrics, not request content. For Dedicated we can keep it in your tenant boundary. We can discuss details in security review, but it’s aggregated telemetry.

[16:30] Ava Chen: Great.

[16:32] Daniel Kim: Also, we use VPC. That’s part of why we’re doing Dedicated.

[16:35] Liam O'Rourke: Yep.

[16:37] Sana Farid: Back to overshoot: would you say 10% is the policy, or do you want to say “never above max, and max is set such that overshoot is at most 10%.”

[16:46] Priya Shah: The second. We’ll set max so that worst-case overshoot is acceptable.

[16:51] Sana Farid: Perfect.

[16:53] Vanessa Ortiz: And we’ll show you “bounded desired vs requested desired.” If requested is frequently above max, that means your max is too tight for your SLO.

[17:03] Mark Feldman: Or the predictor is too aggressive.

[17:05] Vanessa Ortiz: Exactly. We can tell which using reason codes and error metrics.

[17:10] Liam O'Rourke: Can you talk about your acceptable “scale down” timing. Like after market open, do you want it to drop quickly.

[17:17] Ava Chen: We don’t care if it lingers for 30 minutes. We do care if it drops too soon and then we get another micro-spike.

[17:25] Mark Feldman: Yeah, keep it for a bit.

[17:27] Keiko Yamamoto: So we can set a longer scale-down cooldown, shorter scale-up cooldown.

[17:34] Daniel Kim: Does the policy support different cooldowns for up and down.

[17:37] Keiko Yamamoto: Yes.

[17:39] Liam O'Rourke: Cool. And minimum baseline is non-zero.

[17:43] Ava Chen: Definitely non-zero.

[17:45] Mark Feldman: We never want scale-to-zero on Dedicated.

[17:48] Vanessa Ortiz: Agreed. We actually will prevent it unless you explicitly allow, and for Dedicated we typically don’t.

[17:55] Priya Shah: Great.

[17:57] Liam O'Rourke: I want to make sure we address your “recover time.” Mark, you said backlog takes 30 minutes to clear.

[18:03] Mark Feldman: On bad days yes.

[18:05] Sana Farid: That’s an interesting metric. We can measure “time to recover to steady-state latency” after a spike. Predictive should reduce the peak and the recovery time.

[18:16] Mark Feldman: Exactly.

[18:18] Ava Chen: Can you share how you’d implement the predictor. Like is it a separate service.

[18:23] Vanessa Ortiz: At a high level: yes, forecast provider. Autoscaler calls it, gets “recommended desired replicas for time t+lead”. If it’s unavailable, fallback.

[18:35] Daniel Kim: And what SLA on that provider.

[18:38] Vanessa Ortiz: Internally we target something like 99.9 for the interface and we cache last known good forecast. But we also treat it as best-effort; reactive still keeps you safe.

[18:49] Mark Feldman: Caching last known forecast worries me—if it’s stale.

[18:52] Keiko Yamamoto: We only use cached forecast if it’s within staleness window. Otherwise ignore.

[18:58] Mark Feldman: Okay.

[19:00] Liam O'Rourke: Let’s talk about pilot success criteria, even if preliminary. I’m hearing: p95 under 1.2s during market open, no timeouts, and no exceeding max cap.

[19:11] Ava Chen: Yes.

[19:12] Priya Shah: And ideally show us dashboards so we can explain cost and why it scaled.

[19:18] Vanessa Ortiz: We can do a dashboard with: desired vs bounded replicas, bound-hit rate, queue depth, and prediction vs actual demand.

[19:28] Mark Feldman: Bound-hit rate is basically how often you’re hitting the max.

[19:31] Vanessa Ortiz: Exactly.

[19:33] Daniel Kim: If we hit max a lot, then either we need a higher cap or we accept degraded latency.

[19:38] Ava Chen: Right.

[19:40] Liam O'Rourke: That’s the key tradeoff.

[19:42] Sana Farid: For forecast quality, we can also provide “confidence” bands. But we’ve learned those can be confusing.

[19:49] Ava Chen: Yeah, I’d rather keep it simple.

[19:51] Mark Feldman: Confidence can be a trap.

[19:53] Sana Farid: Totally.

[19:55] Liam O'Rourke: We’re at like minute 20. Anything else critical on your side.

[19:59] Priya Shah: Just one more: can we get an audit export for compliance.

[20:03] Liam O'Rourke: We can export audit logs to your SIEM in enterprise plans. For pilot, we can provide logs via API and retention.

[20:11] Ava Chen: Okay.

[20:12] Mark Feldman: Can you confirm that config changes are RBAC’d.

[20:15] Keiko Yamamoto: Yes, update policy endpoints will require admin role. And we can restrict per deployment.

[20:23] Mark Feldman: Great.

[20:24] Liam O'Rourke: Let’s do a quick recap and next steps. I’ll send a template scaling policy recommendation: min baseline 20, max 45 (we’ll refine), predictive lead 15 minutes, scale-up cooldown short, scale-down cooldown longer, step limits. Sana will list metrics we need from you to calibrate. Ava, you’ll share traffic patterns and any schedule inputs. Does that work.

[20:49] Ava Chen: Yes.

[20:50] Mark Feldman: Works.

[20:51] Priya Shah: Yup.

[20:53] Daniel Kim: Yes.

[20:55] Liam O'Rourke: Great. We’ll schedule a follow-up in about a week to align on pilot gating and success metrics.

[21:02] Ava Chen: Perfect.

[21:04] Liam O'Rourke: Thanks all.

[21:06] (Call continues with scheduling / small talk; transcript ends)

Note: Fireflies sometimes truncates the tail end if participants remain connected while scheduling in the calendar.
